Suite CIs are item CIs (n = 65 and 195). Tool selection is pooled over all items and over the canonical suite. Median turn: median over the canonical cases of each case's mean latency. ## Rank uncertainty

Readable configurations only (19 overall, 9 on the NPU paths). Joint cluster bootstrap of the pooled score: each of 10,000 resamples draws 65 base requests with replacement (seed 20261014) for all configurations at once. P(rank 1) is the share of resamples in which the configuration scores highest; a tie for the highest score counts for each tied configuration, so the column can sum to more than 100%. The rank interval holds the central 95% of the resampled ranks, with tied scores sharing the best rank.

## Minimum detectable differences

Paired difference detectable with 80% power by a two-sided test (normal approximation to McNemar), from the observed rate of items whose majority outcome differs, over 260 pooled items. ## Closing braces in text tool calls

Replies without a structured call whose first object opens with {"name" (tagged or bare), cut at the next </tool_call> or the end of the reply. A reply counts as valid after one brace only if appending exactly one '}' makes it valid JSON; nothing else is repaired. The two right-hand counts are variants within 'Other': a final ')' read as the missing '}', and a reply that repeats the call, read up to the second call. Balance is closing minus opening braces in the cut text (count of replies).

## Grader audit

A stratified sample (seed 20261014) of 126 failing and 57 passing repetitions from the 20 configurations whose prompts carried the tools, judged blind by one rater from the request and the reply (A exact; B the requested action, off convention or off schema; C not the requested action or no structured call; D a defensible other reading). Intervals are Wilson 95%; the weighted column reweights each item by the inverse of its sampling probability within its mechanical category and configuration (Kish effective n). ## Modelled turn time with the static prefix cached (a model, not a measurement)

This block is a model, not a measurement. It keeps each turn's decode and non-server time as measured (the median over canonical cases of the per-case mean of client latency minus server prompt time). It assumes that only the user turn and template suffix is read anew, either 50 tokens at the server prefill rate of the shortest agent probe (optimistic) or 100 tokens at the rate of the longest (pessimistic). Reading a short suffix that attends over a cached 2,700-token prefix was not measured, and whether either path can reuse a prefix under GenieX v0.8.0 is not known. Only configurations whose prompts carried the tools are modelled, and requests are single-turn.

The log lines are stamped by the board's clock, the record start by the client's. Every failure's lines are stamped earlier than its own record start, by about the same amount on a given day (2026-10-15: -114, -114 s; 2026-10-16: -184, -181, -180 s; 2026-10-17: -185, -184, -183 s). A board clock behind the client's would give an offset that holds within a day; lines left from an earlier attempt would be unlikely to repeat the same offset across separate models. The records do not say how long a failed load took.

## Measurement quality by serving path

QCS9075 (Dragonwing IQ-9075 EVK, Qualcomm Linux 1.6), GenieX v0.8.0 (QAIRT 2.45, llama.cpp 9425611), 2026-10-14 to 2026-10-17. The thermal rows cover main-matrix runs (diagnostics apart) sampled every 20 s: the hottest of all zones, the hottest CPU zone and the hottest NPU zone, and their margin to the 105 C passive trip. Readiness gates release below 55 C and CPU busy 30%; release values are main matrix. The canonical run's time beyond requests runs from its start to the paraphrase run's start, minus the summed request latency and one warm-up (the median latency); it holds four readiness gates and a few seconds of fixed overhead. Overhead is client latency minus server prefill plus decode, main-matrix requests. Board hours run from each server's start to the end of the last run it served.

The hottest reading was 75.6 C (Qwen3-8B, compiled, paraphrase), and the diagnostic runs reached 73.4 C. The stored thermal summary agrees with its trace in 101 of 102 runs. On the fitted CPU timelines the gates before canonical repetitions 2 and 3 lasted 12.7 to 37.2 s (n=26).

The CPU legs ran with the resident container up. Inside their repetitions the residual over the fitted own load (8.00 active tasks) exceeded +0.5 in 4.5% and +1.0 in 43 (0.5%) of 7,856 intervals (largest +1.88, 26 runs). On the compiled runs, with the container stopped and an own load of 0.80, the deviation from the run median exceeded +0.5 in 6.0% and +1.0 in 9 (0.8%) of 1,154 intervals (largest +1.87, 29 runs). The llama.cpp NPU runs, also with the container stopped, are left out of this contrast: their run medians range from 1.7 to 7.2 active tasks and the deviation exceeded +1.0 in 27.0% of 481 intervals, so their own load varies too much within a run for the median to stand for it. CPU busy at gate release averaged 0.8% (nearest-rank p90 1.4%, n=190) on CPU legs and 0.8% (p90 1.0%, n=170) on both NPU legs, over all runs. Crossing canonical CPU requests whose prefill was more than 3% slower than the fastest repetition with residual load above +0.5 gives [[1, 96], [56, 2377]] (rows slowed and not slowed), one-sided Fisher p = 0.895, Spearman -0.008, n=2,530; the paraphrase suite, against each run's median prefill rate, gives p = 0.414, Spearman 0.040, n=2,530. Setting every prefill to the fastest repetition of its case moves the CPU median turn time by a median 0.3% (max 0.9%) over 13 runs.

Of 10,530 tool-calling requests (1,170 of them diagnostic), 0 returned an error, 0 were retried after an empty reply, 0 empty replies were graded, 0 lacked server timings and 35 reached max_tokens. Server and usage token counts agree in 10,530 (prompt) and 10,530 (completion) of 10,530 requests, and 0 reported cached tokens. Of 720 probe repetitions over 144 lengths, 0 failed, 0 lengths failed calibration, 0 overran max_tokens and 27 had a streamed chunk count different from the token count. Board hours total 62.69; artifact staging, the 9 failed loads (Qwen3-8B waited out the 900 s load check) and the runner's own steps are not in the results and not included.

## Thermal sampler and CPU-path decode

Canonical CPU requests whose three repetitions produced the same number of tokens (n=1,545), by the distance between the decode phase and the nearest sampler ssh session on the fitted timeline. Slowdown is time per token over the fastest repetition of the case. The placebo shifts the sessions by half a sampling period, so its far bins lie near the real sessions and carry their higher rates.

| Distance to a sampler session | Requests | Slowed > 3% | Slowed > 10% | Median slowdown | Placebo: slowed > 3% |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| overlapping | 310 | 172 (55.5%) | 48 | 4.0% | 8 of 258 (3.1%) |
| 0 to 2 s | 307 | 77 (25.1%) | 25 | 0.3% | 6 of 292 (2.1%) |
| 2 to 5 s | 447 | 10 (2.2%) | 6 | 0.1% | 48 of 461 (10.4%) |
| 5 s or more | 481 | 9 (1.9%) | 6 | 0.1% | 206 of 534 (38.6%) |

Overlapping decodes against those 2 s or more away give [[172, 138], [19, 909]], one-sided Fisher p = 4.7e-100. An overlapping decode takes a median 205 ms longer than the fastest repetition (2 ms when 2 s or more away). Each session inside a prefill adds a median 60 ms (12 models, range -9 to 105 ms; 144 ms from the means, which exceed the medians in 11 of 12 models), about 0.3% of CPU compute time at one session per 20.6 s.

These figures rest on the fitted timeline. With every fitted request moved 0.5 s earlier or later, the overlapping decodes number 308 and 316 (180 and 168 slowed by more than 3%; Fisher p = 2.4e-106 and 2.5e-97), and a session inside a prefill adds a median 68 and 58 ms (ranges -4 to 106 and 1 to 104 ms). The counts by distance and the low end of the per-model range move most with the fit.

Turn time is the median over the 65 cases of the mean latency across repetitions, with a bootstrap CI of the median. The CPU over compiled turn-time ratio for the 4B-2507 is 7.11x in version 1, 7.89x in version 2, and the 8B over 4B-2507 ratio on the CPU 1.480 and 1.483. For the chat turn, version 1 applied its 256-token rates to 100 prompt and 300 generated tokens; version 2 measured about 100 prompt and 300 generated tokens, mean +/- sd. The compiled turn is 0.70 s shorter in version 2 on average while answers are 12.2 completion tokens shorter (slope 0.072 s per token over 65 matched cases).

## Status of version 1 findings

Claims are taken from the unpublished version 1 draft report, from docs/PROPOSAL.md and from the version 1 run READMEs. A claim holds when version 2 supports it, is changed when its substance survives with different numbers or qualifiers, and is superseded when version 2 contradicts or replaces it. Intervals are 95% percentile bootstrap intervals over cases or items; p-values are exact McNemar, Holm-adjusted where marked.

| # | Version 1 claim | Source | Status | Version 2 evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| F01 | On the compiled path the NPU reads a prompt about 17 times faster than the CPU and writes at about the same rate (2,044-token prompt: prefill 60 against 1,020 tok/s, decode 13.4 against 13.1 tok/s). | Version 1 draft (unpublished), finding 1; proposal, candidate finding 1 | holds | With one server binary, 5 reps and 128 decode tokens on both paths, prefill is 60.4 against 983 tok/s, a ratio of 16.27x by client timing and 16.92x by server timing (version 1 16.88x), and decode is 13.55 against 13.52 tok/s, a ratio of 0.998 (version 1 0.982, compiled decode averaged over 2048 tokens). At 2,795 tokens the prefill ratio is 17.35x; version 1 has no compiled row there. |
| F02 | An agent turn takes 7.4 s on the compiled path against 52.5 s on the CPU, about 7 times faster. | Version 1 draft (unpublished), finding 1 | holds | The median turn takes 52.93 s on the CPU against 6.71 s compiled (7.89x; version 1 52.51 against 7.39 s, 7.11x), and for Qwen3-8B 78.51 against 9.74 s (8.06x). |
| F03 | A chat turn of 100 prompt and 300 generated tokens is a tie, about 19 s on the CPU and on the compiled path, and about 25 s on the llama.cpp NPU path (extrapolated from the rates at the shortest prompt). | Version 1 draft (unpublished), finding 1; proposal, candidate finding 1 | holds | Measured with about 101 prompt and 300 generated tokens (n = 5), the turn takes 18.37 +/- 0.02 s on the CPU against 17.30 +/- 0.11 s compiled (version 1 estimates 18.9 and 18.7 s). The 4B no longer loads on llama.cpp NPU; for Qwen3-1.7B the chat turn takes 8.56 +/- 0.24 s on the CPU, 9.70 +/- 0.02 s on llama.cpp NPU and 10.93 +/- 0.09 s compiled. |
| F04 | The llama.cpp NPU path is about 6 times faster than the CPU at prefill but slower at decode (386 against 60 tok/s; 7.9 against 13.4 tok/s). | Version 1 draft (unpublished), finding 1 and table 2 | holds | Version 1 measured 6.40x prefill and a decode ratio of 0.59 at 2,044 tokens. The 4B cannot be re-measured, since it no longer loads on this path; for Qwen3-1.7B at 2,041 tokens prefill is 1,000 against 144 tok/s (6.9x) and decode 22.5 against 28.9 tok/s (ratio 0.78). |
| F05 | Changing only the compute unit (same GGUF, same binary) changes nothing: 98.5% on the CPU and on the NPU, with the same failing case and the same wrong answer. | Version 1 draft (unpublished), finding 2 | holds | Version 1 has 0 against 0 discordant cases and 65/65 identical answers. The 4B cannot be re-tested on llama.cpp NPU. In version 2 Qwen3-1.7B scores 90.8 against 90.8% canonical (1 against 1 discordant, 63/65 identical answers) and 68.5 against 68.1% over all 260 items (p = 1.000). |
| F06 | The serving stack changes capability: the compiled build of the same checkpoint scores 92.3% against 98.5% for the GGUF. | Version 1 draft (unpublished), finding 2; 2026-09-15 README | holds | The gap becomes significant only with version 2's paraphrases. CPU-only against compiled-only passes are 5 against 1 in version 1 (p = 0.219); in version 2 canonical 6 against 1, p = 0.125 (Holm 1.000); paraphrase 34 against 10, p = 3.9e-04 (Holm 7.8e-03); all items 40 against 11, p = 5.7e-05 (Holm 5.7e-04), pooled 91.0 against 80.0%. The base Qwen3-4B scores 96.9 against 23.1% canonical, 48 against 0. |
| F07 | On the compiled path tool selection stays at 100%, so every error is the wrong command within the right tool. | Version 1 draft (unpublished), finding 2 | changed | Version 2 compiled tool selection is 96.9% canonical and 86.2% paraphrase; 3.1% of canonical requests return no structured call (cases 37, 42 answer with text in every repetition), against 100.0% tool selection in version 1. |
| F08 | Both builds err at the boundary between a port's administrative state and its PoE power, and the compiled build crosses it more often. | Version 1 draft (unpublished), finding 2 | holds | The PoE mode command answers a request to enable or disable a port in 1 case on the CPU in version 1 and 1 in version 2, and in 3 compiled cases (25, 26, 33) against 2 (25, 33). |
| F09 | A larger model is a net loss on the CPU: Qwen3-8B is about 1.5 times slower than Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 and slightly less accurate (97.2% against 98.5%). | Version 1 draft (unpublished), finding 3; 2026-09-14 and 2026-09-15 READMEs | holds | The deficit is now significant. Version 1 has 2 against 1 discordant cases (p = 1.000); version 2 has canonical 3 against 1, p = 0.625; paraphrase 39 against 7, p = 1.8e-06 (Holm 1.3e-04); all items 91.0 against 78.2%, 42 against 8, p = 1.2e-06 (Holm 2.9e-05). The 8B takes 1.480 times the 4B's turn time in version 1 and 1.483 times in version 2. |
| F10 | The 8B makes a structural error the 4B never makes, returning a command name as the tool name, and picks the PoE mode command for 'configure poe power 15W port 1' in every repetition. | Version 1 draft (unpublished), finding 3 | holds | The 8B names a command as the tool in 4 of 325 requests in version 1, and in 4 of 195 canonical and 44 of 195 paraphrase requests in version 2; the 4B-2507 on the CPU does so in 0 and 0. The 8B fails cases 57, 63 in version 1 and 56, 57, 63 in version 2, with the PoE mode answer to case 57 in both. |
| F11 | Because the 8B cannot use the NPU, its best turn on this board is 77.7 s, against 7.4 s for the 4B on the compiled path. | Version 1 draft (unpublished), finding 3 | superseded | The compiled 8B serves at 9.74 s per turn (84.6% canonical, 77.7% over all items), 1.45 times the compiled 4B-2507's 6.71 s, with no detectable accuracy difference (80.0 against 77.7%, 38 against 32, p = 0.550). |
| F12 | The 8B does not run on this board's NPU by either path, so the largest model the NPU can serve lies between 4B and 8B parameters. | Version 1 draft (unpublished), finding 4 | superseded | On the compiled path a bundle with the same layout (5 parts, largest 1.551 GB) loads in 7.72 s to first reply under GenieX v0.8.0 and scores 84.6% (75.4-92.3) canonical. The claim still holds for llama.cpp NPU, where the 8B load check ends in TimeoutError: timed out at the 900 s limit. |
| F13 | Both NPU load failures come from the per-domain memory-map limit of this silicon (roughly 1 to 1.5 GB). | 2026-09-14 README; version 1 report, finding 4 | superseded | The compiled 8B now loads with the same part sizes, so a fixed limit of the silicon does not explain the version 1 failure. The change cannot be attributed to one cause, since the server (v0.4.0 to v0.8.0), the rebuilt bundle (AI Hub 0.62.2 to 0.64.0) and NPU co-residency (version 1 loaded inside the resident container) all changed. On llama.cpp NPU the 8 failed mappings in the version 2 load logs range from 0.604 to 1.074 GB; the mechanism is unresolved. |

The path loads 4 of 13 models (Qwen3-0.6B, Qwen3-1.7B, Qwen3.5-0.8B, SmolLM2-1.7B-Instruct); GGUF files up to 1,056,782,912 bytes loaded and none from 1,214,873,856 bytes up did (analysis/data/artifacts.json). Version 1's figures (98.5%, 14.48 s) cannot be reproduced on current software. This is probably a regression, but identical artifact and configuration are not proven: version 1 recorded no GGUF hash, and version 2 sets a 4,096-token context that version 1 did not. |
